fullPassage: The recognition of burnout as an occupational phenomenon by the WHO in 2019 marked an important moment in the discourse on workplace mental health. This designation reframes clinical assessment and organizational responsibility, shifting attention to systemic prevention. ① It invites employers to adopt structural interventions rather than relying solely on individual-level remedies. ② In practice, this means clinicians should collaborate with occupational health and leadership to address root causes. ③ Individuals can help themselves recover from burnout by changing patterns that contribute to stress. ④ It signaled a shift away from viewing burnout as a personal failing or a matter of individual resilience, toward understanding it as a structural issue rooted in organizational culture, leadership practices, and the broader socio-economic context of work. ⑤ This reframing is essential, as it opens the door to systemic interventions and policy-level changes rather than placing the burden solely on individuals to cope or adapt.
title: Burnout as a Structural Issue
